video_title: Generics: Reuse Code Without Losing Type Safety
thumbnail_text: Write once, use with any type
core_insight: Generics let you reuse the same code shape for many types while keeping compile-time type safety, by parameterizing the type instead of duplicating code or using unsafe casts.

scenes.voice: Why do we need Generics? Because you want one reusable component that works for many types, but you can't afford runtime cast errors in production.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left shows duplicated IntList, StringList classes, right shows List<Object> with cast warnings.

scenes.voice: Before generics you had two bad options. Duplicate code per type, maintenance nightmare. Or use Object and cast on every read. Reuse yes, safety no.
scenes.visual: Two paths diagram: Duplicate → maintenance cost, Object+cast → runtime error.

scenes.voice: The constraint is clear: reuse code once, enforce type correctness at compile time. That's the problem generics solve.
scenes.visual: Constraint box: reuse once + compile-time safety.

scenes.voice: Generics are parameterized types. You write one definition with T, the compiler creates a type-specific version for each use. Think stencil: shape stays same, material changes.
scenes.visual: Stencil animation stamping Int, User, Event into same List shape.

scenes.voice: In Java, type erasure means T disappears at runtime, so no new T[] and no instanceof List<String>. In C#, reified generics keep T at runtime. The consequence matters for API design.
scenes.visual: Simple flow: GenericDefinition<T> → ConcreteType<X> with erasure note.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[GenericDefinition<T>] -->|compiler| B[ConcreteType<X>]
  B --> C[Shared impl]
  A -.erasure.-> D[Runtime: bound only]

scenes.voice: Use generics where you have same shape of behavior with different data types: Repository<T>, Pipeline<Input,Output>, Result<T,E>. Don't use them to hide different behavior.
scenes.visual: Examples list appearing: Repository<T>, PagedResult<T>, Validator<T>.

scenes.voice: Trade-off: you gain reuse and safety, you pay cognitive complexity. Over-genericizing hurts readability. And erasure forces workarounds like Class<T> tokens.
Mental model: ask is this variation in type or in behavior? If type, parameterize. If behavior, compose.
scenes.visual: Decision diamond: Variation in type? Yes → Generic, No → Separate.

mental_model: Generics are a stencil for type variation. Use a type parameter when multiple types share the same behavior shape. If the behavior itself differs, don't force it into generics.
final_takeaway: Write once with T, get compile-time safety for every type. Parameterize type, not code.
